solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: (& 6ac.) As Trump aims to do in Venezuela? Infantile creature into one military exercise after another

definitions.text: As Trump aims to do in Venezuela
definitions.note: The definition hands over no synonym: it describes a policy and leaves the solver to supply the chant that goes with it, which the question mark admits.

indicators.note: What goes into a thing ends up inside it, so this piece is planted in the middle of what follows rather than beside it.

blocks.note: a drill is the military exercise, rehearsed until it needs no thought
the infantile creature is a baby, and it drops in between
another of the same exercise, so the five letters come round again

explanation.surface: Trump eyeing Venezuela, and a small child loose among one army training session after another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drill baby drill' started as a 2008 Republican convention chant for more oil extraction and Trump revived it; Venezuela sits on the largest proven oil reserves on earth. The military sense of drill is the decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Drill baby drill is the chant for pumping oil out of the ground, which is what Trump wants done to Venezuela's reserves.

clue.text: In here a gangster president is revealed

indicators.note: What is in the words that follow lies within their letters rather than standing beside them.
Something revealed was there all along and only needed uncovering, so the letters are read straight off as written.

blocks.note: six letters running on across the join of the two words, starting two in

explanation.surface: A president turning out to be among the gangsters in this room.
explanation.walkthrough: Ronald Reagan played gangsters in Hollywood before he reached the White House, so the company the surface puts him in is pointed. The run straddles two word breaks, which is where a hidden answer is hardest to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Reagan is one American president among many, so the bare word names the answer by example rather than defining it.

clue.text: Get behind with the news of Miss T? That's painful

blocks.note: to miss something is to lose it
the initial as the clue prints it
what you say out loud when something hurts

explanation.surface: Falling behind on Miss T's news, and how much that smarts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's painful' sits at the end of the clue where a definition usually sits, and it is an exclamation instead. Miss T does nothing but lend her initial.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose touch with someone is to stop hearing anything of them, which is exactly what being behind with their news amounts to.

clue.text: Herb: "Is blocking Keir's lot on the up?"

indicators.note: To block something is to sit in its way, so this piece jams into the middle of the other instead of queueing behind it.
In a down entry what is on the up is read from the bottom, so the letters come out back to front.

blocks.note: Keir Starmer leads Labour, three letters for the party in every British headline
the little word taken whole, jammed in after the party's first letter

explanation.surface: A man named Herb asking whether Keir Starmer's party is on the rise.
explanation.walkthrough: Basil and Herb are both men's names, which is how the definition hides in plain sight at the front. The quotation marks make the rest sound like a question rather than an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Basil is the sweet-smelling leaf of Italian cooking, a herb in the plain kitchen sense.

clue.text: Contemptible type of charmer introduces new date

blocks.note: a belle is a beauty, and so a charmer
n is the standard short form of new
d is the short form a diary uses for date

explanation.surface: A charming sort presenting his latest romantic conquest.
explanation.walkthrough: Everything before the answer stays polite: the belle, the new date, the introductions. British abuse supplies the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A bellend is British abuse for an obnoxious idiot, the insult borrowed from the end of the penis.

clue.text: see 1ac.
Clever to go topless, being fit

indicators.note: To go topless is to lose what covers the top, and the top of a word in a down entry is the letter it starts with.

blocks.note: clever is bright, six letters to start from

explanation.surface: A bright young thing stripping off and looking in good shape.
explanation.walkthrough: Fit means athletic in the surface and sound or proper in the answer — not feeling right, putting things right. Three plain adjectives in a row give no sign that the middle phrase is an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Right in the sense of sound and in order is what a person who is fit for something is, as in fit to travel.

clue.text: Drink, right, taken by gutless Lammy in recent times?

indicators.note: A gutless word has had its insides pulled out, leaving only the letters standing at either end.

blocks.note: a latte is the milky coffee
r is the usual abbreviation for right
the outer letters of the name, its middle taken out

explanation.surface: David Lammy putting drinks away of late, with no stomach for them.
explanation.walkthrough: David Lammy is a senior Labour minister and a regular target of this puzzle. The comma'd 'right' reads as a conversational tag, which is what hides a single letter in the middle of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Latterly means in the later part of a stretch of time, and so of late — recently, as against how things were before.

clue.text: State requires 1001 undercover soldiers

blocks.note: the thousand is k, as in a salary, and the one is an, written in that order
the SAS are Britain's special forces regiment, the soldiers sent in covertly

explanation.surface: A state demanding a thousand and one secret troops.
explanation.walkthrough: A number in a clue usually wants Roman numerals, and this one does not. Kansas is the flat plains state Dorothy spends The Wizard of Oz trying to get back to.
explanation.definitionFit: Kansas is one of the fifty United States, so the bare word names the answer by example.

clue.text: Fired, one needs access to take legal action

blocks.note: a fired stove is a lit one
the single stroke that writes one
a gate is the way in

explanation.surface: A sacked employee who still needs to get into the building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fired' pulls hard towards being sacked, which is the story the surface tells; the wordplay means set alight. Access is a gate here, not a password.
explanation.definitionFit: To litigate is to go to law over a dispute, taking it to court rather than settling it privately.

clue.text: Temper hit the president on ditching Pence

indicators.note: To ditch a thing is to throw it out, so the letter named goes from the word it was sitting in.

blocks.note: to tan somebody is to beat them
Trump is the president, and he ends a letter short here
p is pence, the British coin, and Mike Pence was Trump's vice-president — that letter is the one thrown out

explanation.surface: A president flying off the handle the moment he drops Pence.
explanation.walkthrough: One word does two jobs: Pence is the running mate discarded in 2024 and the penny's abbreviation naming the letter to lose. Tanning a hide is beating it, which is where the slang for a thrashing comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: A tantrum is an outburst of temper, the foot-stamping kind a child throws and an adult is mocked for.

clue.text: Lozenge from Dicky, covered by Pulp

indicators.note: To be covered by something is to have it over you on every side, so this piece finishes up inside the other.

blocks.note: pulp something and what you have is a paste
dicky is British for poorly — a dicky heart is an unreliable one

explanation.surface: A throat sweet from a man called Dicky, buried under pulp.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P invites you to hear the band, and Pulp is a verb. Dicky is a first name in the surface and British for out of sorts in the wordplay — a dicky ticker is a weak heart.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastille is the small soft sweet you suck for a sore throat, which is what a lozenge is.

clue.text: (& 20dn.) Genitals? Hell!

definitions.note: 'Hell' is one place where the answer is plural, but the underworld has always been spoken of as the regions below, the way the tropics names one belt of the earth in the plural.

blocks.note: the polite British way of pointing at the parts below the waist without naming them
nether means lower, and the lower world is where hell has always been placed

explanation.surface: Someone raising the subject of the private parts and swearing in the same breath.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses are downward: the body below the waist and the world below this one. The exclamation mark dresses the second definition up as an oath so it reads as a reaction rather than a meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The nether regions are the parts below — the body's lower half in polite embarrassment, and the underworld in older usage, which is hell.

clue.text: Tories all but due for a transformation – Liz Truss's role?

definitions.note: The definition offers no synonym: it names a politician and asks what she is, and the question mark admits that the solver has to supply the word.

indicators.note: All but means all except the last scrap, so the word beside it stops one letter short of its end.
Something up for transformation is not going to come out in the shape it went in, and nor do these letters.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder
due handed over all but its final letter

explanation.surface: The Conservatives almost ready for a makeover, and the part Liz Truss plays in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Liz Truss lasted forty-nine days as prime minister in 2022 and has been outside her own party's mainstream ever since. 'All but' is the only fiddly instruction in the clue and it is easy to read as mere emphasis.
explanation.definitionFit: An outsider is the one who stands apart from the group and, in betting, the runner nobody backs — either way, where Liz Truss ended up.

clue.text: Danes forced to be crushed by a totalitarian force – tragedy

definitions.note: A tragedy is the event and sadness the feeling it leaves; the setter uses one for the other in the loose way an exclamation of grief does.

indicators.note: To be crushed by something is to be squeezed inside it, with the weight bearing down on either side.

blocks.note: the SS were Hitler's paramilitary corps, known by those two letters everywhere
five letters of fodder

explanation.surface: Danes crushed under a totalitarian army, and the tragedy of it.
explanation.walkthrough: Denmark was occupied by Nazi Germany from 1940, so the surface is history rather than invention. 'Force' appears twice in the clue doing entirely different jobs, once as an instruction and once as a troop.
explanation.definitionFit: Sadness is the grief a tragedy leaves behind, the clue naming the event and asking for the feeling that goes with it.

clue.text: "GREENLAND'S FIRST THEN THE WHOLE SHEBANG – IT'S GROWTH!"

indicators.note: What comes first in a word is the letter at its front, before any of the rest.

blocks.note: the letter Greenland begins with
the whole shebang is the lot of it, every last bit

explanation.surface: A shouted boast about taking Greenland first and then everything else, billed as growth.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals are the joke: this is a presidential post, not a setter's voice. A gall is the hard swelling a wasp or fungus raises on an oak, so the growth is a lump rather than an economy.
explanation.definitionFit: A gall is the woody swelling an insect or fungus provokes on a plant, a growth in the lump sense rather than the economic one.

clue.text: Hot dog, gin cocktail and it's bed for me

definitions.note: The definition is not a synonym but a remark: the answer is the word said in place of 'it's bed for me' on leaving the room.

indicators.note: A cocktail is poured and shaken together, so what goes in does not come out in the order it went.

blocks.note: the nine letters of the snack and the spirit re-set

explanation.surface: A late snack and a gin before turning in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cocktail' reads as a third thing on the tray rather than an instruction, which is the whole trick. Nine letters of fodder sitting in two short words are easy to walk straight past.
explanation.definitionFit: Goodnight is what you say on going up to bed, so the clue gives the sentiment and asks for the word that carries it.

clue.text: An undergarment caught in crack leads to mockery

indicators.note: What is caught in something is stuck inside it, held between the letters it went in through.

blocks.note: a crack at something is a try at it
the indefinite article, and a is the same article before a consonant
a vest is the undergarment

explanation.surface: Underwear caught in a crack, and the ridicule that follows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' is a gap in the surface and an attempt in the wordplay — having a crack at it. A travesty was first a burlesque, a serious work dressed up in ridiculous clothes, which is where the underwear fits.
explanation.definitionFit: A travesty is a grotesque imitation of the real thing — a travesty of justice makes a mockery of the courts.

clue.text: Saucy underwear Charles conceals

indicators.note: What conceals something has it hidden inside, spelt out in order and waiting to be read off.

blocks.note: four letters straddling the gap between the two words, the last two of one and the first two of the next

explanation.surface: Charles keeping some risqué underwear out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: Arch means knowing and teasing — an arch smile, an arch remark — not curved or chief, which are the senses that come to mind first. Charles is there to be looked at, not looked up.
explanation.definitionFit: Arch describes a knowingly playful, faintly suggestive manner, which is what saucy names in a person's tone.

clue.text: Can act increasingly like a tear-arse, by the sound of it

indicators.note: By the sound of it asks you to trust the ear over the spelling, so say the words and hear what else they make.

blocks.note: a tear-arse is British for someone who rushes everywhere, so acting more like one is darting more

explanation.surface: Someone working up to behaving like a headlong lunatic.
explanation.walkthrough: The can is prison in slang, so one short word at the front carries the definition. Dartmoor is the grim Victorian jail out on the Devon moors, the name a British reader reaches for when they mean a hard prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Dartmoor stands for prison itself in British use, the way 'the can' does in slang — the jail's name borrowed for the institution.

clue.text: se 13ac.
Able to swallow drugs at a party in Ibiza?

indicators.note: To swallow a thing is to take it right inside you, which is where these letters end up.

blocks.note: fit is able in the sense of being up to the job
e is ecstasy and a handful of tablets are es
the article's single letter, tacked on at the end

explanation.surface: Somebody capable of putting away drugs at a party on Ibiza.
explanation.walkthrough: Naming Ibiza is the setter saying which language the word for party will be in. 'Swallow' has to be taken as an instruction exactly where the surface makes it literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiesta is a Spanish festival or party, and the Balearic island in the clue says the word wanted is the Spanish one.

clue.text: Approach Madonna's rear spot

indicators.note: The rear of a word is the end of it, so the letter taken is the one at the back.

blocks.note: the last letter of the name
the place where a gig or a match is staged

explanation.surface: Getting up close to a blemish on Madonna's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot' is a place, not a pimple, and Madonna is only a word with a letter on the end of it. An avenue of trees is the grand approach to a country house, which is where the sense the definition wants comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: An avenue is the tree-lined way up to a house, and by extension any approach — an avenue of enquiry is a way in.

clue.text: Deny bust overlaps top of robe, being geekish

indicators.note: A bust thing is a broken one, and broken letters do not lie in the order they were set in.
What overlaps something lies across it with part on either side, so the letter named goes in between.
The top of a word is the letter it starts with, the one sitting above the rest.

blocks.note: four letters of fodder
the letter robe starts with

explanation.surface: A bust spilling over the top of a robe, and someone denying it.
explanation.walkthrough: The crude surface is doing its job: 'bust' looks like a body and is an instruction to break letters up. 'Deny' sits where a definition would and is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Nerdy describes someone absorbed in unfashionable enthusiasms, which is what calling a person geekish says about them.

clue.text: Massive show against Conservative leader

indicators.note: A leader goes at the head of the rest, so the letter taken is the one at the front of the word.

blocks.note: a gig is a show, a night's booking for a band
anti means against
the letter the party's name starts with

explanation.surface: A huge protest concert staged against the leader of the Conservatives.
explanation.walkthrough: The Conservative leader is a person in the surface and a single letter in the wordplay, and the clue never has to say who. 'Against' goes in whole, which is rarer than a clue this politically loaded suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Gigantic means of giant size, a plain swap for massive, the word coming from the Giants of Greek myth.

clue.text: Sombre end of ruling party

indicators.note: The end of a word is its final letter, the one the rest runs out at.

blocks.note: the last letter of ruling
a rave is an all-night dance party

explanation.surface: The last days of the governing party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruling party' reads as one phrase and is two separate jobs. Grave is sombre as an adjective and a burial plot as a noun, and the clue's talk of endings leans on both without saying so.
explanation.definitionFit: Grave means serious to the point of gloom — a grave expression, grave news — which is what sombre describes.

clue.text: Drugs taken by hacks – nothing on drink

blocks.note: e is ecstasy and es is a few of them
the press are the journalists, hacks as Fleet Street calls itself
the round letter stands in for zero

explanation.surface: Journalists on drugs, with nothing to say about drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash is the only sign the clue changes direction halfway through. An espresso is coffee forced through the grounds under pressure, which is what the Italian name is saying.
explanation.definitionFit: An espresso is a small strong coffee, so the definition names the class the answer is one kind of.

clue.text: Dignified, USA? Gut-wrenching!

indicators.note: To wrench a thing is to twist it out of the position it was fixed in, and these letters are twisted out of theirs.

blocks.note: the six letters of the country and the gut re-set

explanation.surface: A stomach-turning question about whether the USA has any dignity left.
explanation.walkthrough: The month and the adjective are spelt alike but said differently — au-GUST for the imposing sense. 'Gut-wrenching' splits down the hyphen, half of it fodder and half of it the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: August means imposing and venerable — an august body, an august presence — which is dignity carried with weight.

clue.text: Organ on right side of Cyclops's balls

indicators.note: In an across entry the right-hand side is the finish, so the piece named before it is written second.

blocks.note: Cyclops sets this puzzle, so his own word for himself is the first person
the eye is the organ, and the Cyclops of myth has only the one

explanation.surface: Cyclops pointing out the organ to the right of his own nether equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter signs himself Cyclops and means himself whenever the name appears in a clue. 'My eye!' is dated British for rubbish — all my eye and Betty Martin — which is the job 'balls' does more bluntly.
explanation.definitionFit: 'My eye!' is an old British cry of disbelief, meaning nonsense, which is exactly what calling something balls means.

clue.text: Key Republicans' focus after senate is corrupted

indicators.note: The focus of a word is its centre, the one letter with as many on one side as the other.
What comes after goes behind, so this letter is written at the end of what precedes it.
What is corrupted has been tampered with, and these letters come out in a tampered order.

blocks.note: the eight letters of those two words re-set
the middle letter of the eleven in Republicans

explanation.surface: What the Republicans are concentrating on now the senate has been bought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' sits alone at the front, where a solver reads it as part of the politics rather than as the definition. Republicans has eleven letters, an odd number, so it has a true middle one to give.
explanation.definitionFit: Key as an adjective means indispensable — the key witness, the key question — which is what essential names.
